label.INDMHEALTH: Percentage with GHQ12 scores ≥ 4 (signifying possible mental health problem)

result.label: Indicator - Mental health
note:
[b]Mental health[/b]

[b]How do we measure this?[/b]
Percentage aged 16+ with General Health Questionnaire-12 (GHQ12) scores greater than or equal to 4 (signifying possible mental health problem). For this indicator a lower figure is better.

[b]Source[/b]
Health Survey Northern Ireland, Department of Health
[url=https://www.health-ni.gov.uk/topics/health-survey-northern-ireland]https://www.health-ni.gov.uk/topics/health-survey-northern-ireland[/url] 

[b]Impact of Covid-19[/b]
Due to the coronavirus (Covid-19) pandemic, data collection for the 2020/21, 2021/22 and 2022/23 Health Survey Northern Ireland moved from face-to-face interviewing (with GHQ12 administered as a self-completion module) to telephone mode. Face-to-face interviewing was reinstated alongside telephone interviewing in June 2023, thus the survey adopted a mixed mode methodology for 2023/24 and 2024/25. Any changes within the 2024/25 data compared with previous years should be considered in the context of all of the above and caution should be exercised when drawing conclusions from the findings. Further details on these changes can be found at the start of the Health Survey Northern Ireland 2024/25 report, entitled ‘Health Survey Northern Ireland 2024/25 - Things users need to know'.

[b]Further information[/b]
1. The GHQ12 information is collected as part of the [url=https://www.health-ni.gov.uk/topics/health-survey-northern-ireland]Health Survey Northern Ireland[/url]. The statistics presented here relate to the proportion of adult respondents that scored four or more on the GHQ12 scale and are referred to as having a ‘high GHQ12 score’. A high score signifies a possible mental health problem.
2. In 2018/19, as part of an ongoing methodological review, a revised weighting methodology has been adopted. For comparison purposes, the previous years have been updated to reflect the revised methodology.
3. Data is not available for 2012/13 as the questions were not included in the survey. 
4. Prior to the commencement of the Health Survey NI in 2010/11, data were collected in the NI Continuous Household Survey (2009/10) and the NI Health and Wellbeing Survey (2005/06).
5. Respondents are aged 16+.
6. As the 2020/21, 2021/22 and 2022/23 health surveys were carried out in telephone mode and the 2023/24 and 2024/25 health surveys were in mixed mode, results may not be fully comparable with those collected as self-completion during a household interview.
7. For more information on this data please contact the data provider [url=mailto:phirb@health-ni.gov.uk]Public Health Information & Research Branch, Information Analysis Directorate, DoH[/url] or further information on the Health Survey is available online at [url=https://www.health-ni.gov.uk/topics/health-survey-northern-ireland]https://www.health-ni.gov.uk/topics/health-survey-northern-ireland[/url]

[b]Sex[/b]
8. In 2024/25, females were more likely than males to have a high GHQ12 score. The proportion of males with a high GHQ12 score was similar to the comparison year of 2021/22, while for females it had fallen from 25% in 2021/22 to 20% in 2024/25. It should be noted that there was a significant worsening during 2020/21 due to the pandemic. Considering the longer term trend, the proportion of both males and females scoring highly remains similar to their respective levels in 2010/11. Further information on how to interpret the survey estimates and detail on the sample size and confidence intervals is available to [url=https://view.officeapps.live.com/op/view.aspx?src=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.health-ni.gov.uk%2Fsites%2Fdefault%2Ffiles%2F2026-05%2Fghq12-pfg-tables-hsni.xlsx&wdOrigin=BROWSELINK]download here[/url]. 

[b]Age[/b]
9. In 2024/25, respondents in the 50-64 age group were the more likely to have a high GHQ12 score than those aged 16-49 and 65-74. Those aged 50-64 saw a decrease from the comparison year of 2021/22, while there was no change for all other age groups. Considering the longer term trend, estimates for those aged 16-49 have fallen, while estimates for those aged 50-74 have remained at broadly similar levels to 2010/11 and the estimate for those aged 75+ has increased. Further information on how to interpret the survey estimates and detail on the sample size and confidence intervals is available to [url=https://view.officeapps.live.com/op/view.aspx?src=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.health-ni.gov.uk%2Fsites%2Fdefault%2Ffiles%2F2026-05%2Fghq12-pfg-tables-hsni.xlsx&wdOrigin=BROWSELINK]download here[/url].
10. Due to decreasing numbers of respondents aged 16-24 completing the Health Survey, age-groups 16-24 and 25-34 have been combined to form 16-34. Previous data has been updated to reflect this change.

[b]Marital status[/b]
11. In 2024/25, respondents who were married or in a civil partnership were less likely to have a high GHQ12 score than those that were single or divorced. In comparison with 2021/22, the rate for those that were married or in a civil partnership was lower in 2024/25, while all others were at a similar level. Considering the longer term trend, in comparison with 2010/11, there was a decrease for those who were married or in a civil partnership, while all others were at a similar level. Further information on how to interpret the survey estimates and detail on the sample size and confidence intervals is available to [url=https://view.officeapps.live.com/op/view.aspx?src=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.health-ni.gov.uk%2Fsites%2Fdefault%2Ffiles%2F2026-05%2Fghq12-pfg-tables-hsni.xlsx&wdOrigin=BROWSELINK]download here[/url]. 
12. The marital status categories were amended from 2013/14 onwards to capture more detail on civil partnerships. It is not considered that this will have had an impact on the data.
13. Some estimates have been suppressed due to small sample sizes (less than 101 respondents).

[b]Religion[/b]
14. In 2024/25, there was no difference between Catholics and Protestants in terms of scoring highly on the GHQ12. In comparison with 2021/22, rates for Catholics and Protestants were at a similar level, while there was a decrease noted for the Other/No religion/Not known category. Considering the longer term trend, estimates remain at similar levels to 2010/11 for Catholics and Protestants, while the estimate is lower for those in the Other/No religion/Not known category. Further information on how to interpret the survey estimates and detail on the sample size and confidence intervals is available to [url=https://view.officeapps.live.com/op/view.aspx?src=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.health-ni.gov.uk%2Fsites%2Fdefault%2Ffiles%2F2026-05%2Fghq12-pfg-tables-hsni.xlsx&wdOrigin=BROWSELINK]download here[/url]. 
15. 'Other' includes those with any other religion other than Catholic and Protestant, those with no religion and those who did not state a religion.

[b]Deprivation[/b]
16. A consistent gap remains between the most and least deprived areas, with respondents in the most deprived areas (24%) continuing to be more likely to have a high GHQ12 score than those in the least deprived areas (14%). In comparison with 2021/22, the rate was lower for those in both the most and the least deprived areas, while it was at a similar level for all other quintiles. Considering the longer term trend, estimates remain at similar levels to 2010/11. Further information on how to interpret the survey estimates and detail on the sample size and confidence intervals is available to [url=https://view.officeapps.live.com/op/view.aspx?src=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.health-ni.gov.uk%2Fsites%2Fdefault%2Ffiles%2F2026-05%2Fghq12-pfg-tables-hsni.xlsx&wdOrigin=BROWSELINK]download here[/url]. 
17. All figures up to and including 2017/18 are defined according to the 2010 NIMDM; figures from 2018/19 onwards are based on the 2017 NIMDM. More information on the NI Multiple Deprivation Measures can be found on the NISRA website: [url=https://www.nisra.gov.uk/statistics/people-and-communities/deprivation]https://www.nisra.gov.uk/statistics/people-and-communities/deprivation[/url] 

[b]Urban Rural[/b]
18. In 2024/25, respondents in urban areas (20%) were more likely than those in rural areas (14%) to have a high GHQ12 score. In comparison with 2021/22, the rate has fallen for urban areas, while it remains at a similar level for those living in rural and mixed urban/rural areas. Considering the longer term trend, the estimate for those in rural areas has fallen from 2010/11, while the estimate for those in urban areas is at a similar level. Further information on how to interpret the survey estimates and detail on the sample size and confidence intervals is available to [url=https://view.officeapps.live.com/op/view.aspx?src=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.health-ni.gov.uk%2Fsites%2Fdefault%2Ffiles%2F2026-05%2Fghq12-pfg-tables-hsni.xlsx&wdOrigin=BROWSELINK]download here[/url]. 
19. Figures up to and including 2015 are defined according 2005 Urban Rural classification; figures from 2016 onwards are based on the 2015 Urban Rural classification. More information on Urban Rural classifications can be found here: [url=https://www.nisra.gov.uk/support/geography/urban-rural-classification]https://www.nisra.gov.uk/support/geography/urban-rural-classification[/url]
